name: Peg-MGF (mechano growth factor)

card.summary: A pegylated synthetic version of the IGF-1Ec peptide sold as a research chemical for muscle growth; human evidence is absent and it is WADA-banned.
card.note: Not approved for any use; WADA-prohibited; research raises carcinogenicity questions.

quick.overview:
Mechano growth factor (MGF, or IGF-1Ec) is a 24-amino-acid peptide the body produces by splicing of the IGF-1 gene during muscle repair after exercise. Peg-MGF is a synthetic, pegylated version sold online as a research chemical and used by some bodybuilders for muscle gain.

The published evidence is laboratory and animal work. Reference sources report no human clinical trial results for MGF as a muscle-building drug.
quick.mechanism: Natural MGF is described as acting in muscle repair and is rapidly degraded in the body. Pegylation and amino-acid substitutions in synthetic versions are intended to improve stability.
quick.risks: Not approved as a medicine anywhere. The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits MGF. A 2020 review raised concerns about potential carcinogenicity, and human safety data are not available.

lead: Mechano growth factor (MGF), also called IGF-1Ec, is a naturally occurring 24-amino-acid peptide produced from the IGF-1 gene during muscle repair after exercise, and is described as having anabolic effects.[1] PEG-MGF is a pegylated synthetic form sold as a research chemical.[1]

Research on MGF is mainly laboratory and animal work covering muscle repair and aging, signaling in muscle growth, neuroprotection and cardiac protection, and reviews have questioned its role in repair.[1] No human clinical trial results are reported in the reference article, which also notes the World Anti-Doping Agency has banned MGF and that a 2020 review raised concerns about potential carcinogenicity.[1]

paras: MGF is the C-terminal fragment associated with the IGF-1Ec splice variant and is produced in muscle after loading or damage.[1] Natural MGF is broken down quickly in the body, and synthetic versions often incorporate unnatural D-amino acids in the central region for metabolic stability, and in some products the tyrosine is pegylated.[1]

Cited studies address muscle repair and aging, signaling pathways in muscle growth, neuroprotection after brain ischemia, protection of heart tissue after infarction, neurogenesis in aging mouse brains and nerve regeneration.[1] These are laboratory and animal findings. Reviews by some authors have questioned MGF's role in repair, and a 2020 review raised concern about possible carcinogenicity.[1]

MGF's anabolic reputation has led to illicit use by athletes, and the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits it; doping-control detection methods were published in 2009, 2014 and 2017.[1] In bodybuilding communities, Peg-MGF is sold and discussed as a research peptide, often alongside growth hormone or IGF-1 related products.

No studies found. Research on MGF is limited to laboratory and animal work. A registered trial of a different long-acting growth hormone product, pegylated somatropin, in short-stature children is unrelated to Peg-MGF.[2]

timeline.event: Goldspink publishes a review on muscle response to stretch and overload, an early source in the MGF literature cited by Wikipedia.[1]
Doping-control research on MGF detection begins appearing in the literature.[1]
A review raises concerns about MGF's potential carcinogenicity.[1]

lore.intro: Peg-MGF is discussed in muscle-building communities as a localized growth peptide.

claims.claim: Peg-MGF triggers muscle growth after training
claims.believers: Users say it activates satellite cells and supports hypertrophy because MGF is produced after exercise.
claims.experts: Evidence is laboratory and animal work, and reviews have questioned the role of MGF in repair; no human trials are reported.[1]

claims.claim: Pegylation makes MGF active long enough to work
claims.believers: Sellers argue pegylation extends the short half-life of natural MGF.
claims.experts: Natural MGF is rapidly metabolized, and no human pharmacology data for pegylated versions are cited.[1]
